cited_works.title: &lt;i&gt;In Vivo &lt;/i&gt; Imaging of Biophoton Emission in the Whole Brain of Mice
cited_works.abstract: In recent years, studies have demonstrated that biophoton is a medium for the transmission and processing of neural information. However, such studies were mainly carried out by using brain slices combined with biophoton imaging technology, while there are few reports on in vivo brain biophoton imaging. In this study, the ultraweak biophoton imaging system (UBIS) was employed to carry out an in vivo biophoton imaging for the whole brain of mice. It was found that the biophoton emission of whole brain in the slightly anesthetized mice was significantly higher than that of the background, suggesting that the brain of living mouse emits a certain intensity of stable biophotons. The biophoton imaging established in this study for the in vivo mouse whole brain may provide a new technical method for further study of the relationship between the biophoton and brain functions, and give new ideas for developing diagnostic method of neuropsychiatric diseases.

cited_works.title: Exploring ultraweak photon emissions as optical markers of brain activity

UPEs are triggered by neurotransmitters and biophysical stimuli, but they are also generated by cells at rest and can be passively recorded using modern photodetectors in dark environments. UPEs play a role in cell-to-cell communication, and neural cells might even have waveguiding properties that support optical channels. However, it remains uncertain whether passive light emissions can be used to infer brain states as electric and magnetic fields do for encephalography. We present evidence that brain UPEs differ from background light in spectral and entropic properties, respond dynamically to tasks and stimulation, and correlate moderately with brain rhythms. We discuss these findings in the context of other neuroimaging methods, the potential of new measurement parameters, the limitations of light-based readouts, and the possibility of developing a platform to readout functional brain states: photoencephalography.

cited_works.abstract: Background: Although clinically, Alzheimer's disease (AD) and vascular dementia (VaD) are the two major types of dementia, it is unclear whether the biophotonic activities associated with cognitive impairments in these diseases share common pathological features. Methods: We used the ultraweak biophoton imaging system (UBIS) and synaptosomes prepared by modified percoll method to directly evaluate the functional changes in synapses and neural circuits in AD and VaD model animals. Results: We found that biophotonic activities induced by glutamate were significantly reduced and spectral blueshifted in synaptosomes and brain slices. Conclusion: Our findings suggest that AD and VaD pathology present similar but complex changes in biophotonic activities and transmission at synapses and neural circuits, implying that communications and information processing of biophotonic signals in the brain are crucial for advanced cognitive functions.

cited_works.title: The impact of ketamine and thiopental anesthesia on ultraweak photon emission and oxidative-nitrosative stress in rat brains
cited_works.abstract: Anesthetics such as ketamine and thiopental, commonly used for inducing unconsciousness, have distinct effects on neuronal activity, metabolism, and cardiovascular and respiratory systems. Ketamine increases heart rate and blood pressure while preserving respiratory function, whereas thiopental decreases both and can cause respiratory depression. This study investigates the impact of ketamine (100 mg/kg) and thiopental (45 mg/kg) on ultraweak photon emission (UPE), oxidative-nitrosative stress, and antioxidant capacity in isolated rat brains. To our knowledge, no previous study has investigated and compared UPE in the presence and absence of anesthesia. Here, we compare the effects of ketamine and thiopental anesthetics with each other and with a non-anesthetized control group. Ketamine increased UPE, lipid peroxidation, and antioxidant enzyme activity while reducing thiol levels. Conversely, thiopental decreased UPE, oxidative markers, and antioxidant enzyme activity, while increasing thiol levels. UPE was negatively correlated with thiol levels and positively correlated with oxidative stress markers. These findings suggest that the contrasting effects of ketamine and thiopental on UPE are linked to their differing impacts on brain oxidative stress and antioxidant capacity. This research suggests a potential method to monitor brain oxidative stress via UPE during anesthesia, and opens up new ways for understanding and managing anesthetic effects.

cited_works.title: Revisiting Claims of Extracranial Biophoton Detection from the Human Brain
cited_works.abstract: Ultraweak photon emission, also referred to as biological autoluminescence or biophoton emission, is the spontaneous emission of extremely low levels of light from a broad range of biological systems. Recent studies have reported that UPE measured extracranially can serve as a potential noninvasive biomarker of brain activity. Here, we show that this interpretation suffers from serious problems. We show that, when observed under properly dark conditions, the UPE from the head is much weaker than what is reported in certain papers on "brain UPE" from human heads. We also show that the large signals reported in these studies can be explained by background light contamination. Furthermore, photons with wavelengths <600 nm are strongly attenuated by scalp and skull tissues, and longer wavelengths fall largely outside the effective spectral sensitivity of the photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) used. As a consequence, even if UPE from the head is detected under properly background-free conditions, it is likely to be dominated by emission from the scalp rather than from the brain, certainly as long as PMTs are used. Our results emphasize the importance of careful experimental design to make genuine progress on this important question.

cited_works.title: Human high intelligence is involved in spectral redshift of biophotonic activities in the brain
cited_works.abstract: Human beings hold higher intelligence than other animals on Earth; however, it is still unclear which brain properties might explain the underlying mechanisms. The brain is a major energy-consuming organ compared with other organs. Neural signal communications and information processing in neural circuits play an important role in the realization of various neural functions, whereas improvement in cognitive function is driven by the need for more effective communication that requires less energy. Combining the ultraweak biophoton imaging system (UBIS) with the biophoton spectral analysis device (BSAD), we found that glutamate-induced biophotonic activities and transmission in the brain, which has recently been demonstrated as a novel neural signal communication mechanism, present a spectral redshift from animals (in order of bullfrog, mouse, chicken, pig, and monkey) to humans, even up to a near-infrared wavelength (∼865 nm) in the human brain. This brain property may be a key biophysical basis for explaining high intelligence in humans because biophoton spectral redshift could be a more economical and effective measure of biophotonic signal communications and information processing in the human brain.

rationale.step: The field's own critical review of UPE photocount statistics states that claims about the statistical properties of UPE are highly controversial (in contrast to intensity and spectrum, where there is some consensus) and closes by saying detectors with properties closer to ideal detectors may bring at least partial answers to open questions about UPE statistics; this locates the controversy in the detector, not the source.

Empirically, the measured Fano factor of UPE from germinating mung bean is reported to approach the Poisson value as the signal-to-dark-count ratio increases, which is a direct observation that the reported excess is a function of dark-count fraction rather than of the source.

Fano factors near but above 1 (e.g. mean count 27.25, variance 34.01, F ~ 1.25) are reported from germinating-seed measurements and are read in the field as indicating photocount statistics departing from Poisson, and departure from Poisson is explicitly treated as an indication of non-classical light.

Derivation. For a source with mean photon number n and Fano factor F_s, Bernoulli detection with efficiency eta gives detected counts m with mean S = eta*n and Var(m) = eta^2*Var(n) + eta*(1-eta)*n, hence F_d = 1 + eta*(F_s - 1). Adding independent Poissonian dark counts of mean D gives total mean S+D and total variance S*F_d + D, so F_meas = 1 + [S/(S+D)]*eta*(F_s - 1). Inverting: F_s - 1 = (F_meas - 1)*(S+D)/(eta*S).

Numerical consequence. A single reported F_meas = 1.25 maps to F_s = 3.5 for eta = 0.20 and S/(S+D) = 0.5, but to F_s = 1.31 for eta = 0.90 and S/(S+D) = 0.9 - a factor-of-8 spread in the inferred source excess (2.5 vs 0.31) driven entirely by two instrument parameters. Those two parameters differ by exactly this much across the detectors actually in use: quantum efficiency 0.23 with 22 dark counts/s for a head-UPE PMT, 0.70 with <25 cps for a SPAD module, and >0.90 with ~1e-4 dark current for a back-illuminated EMCCD.

The three detector classes named in the scope are all in current use on exactly these preparations, so the parallel measurement is buildable today: cooled PMT photon counters, SiPM/SPAD photon-counting modules, and EMCCD/CCD cameras with >90% visible QE.

Poissonian dark counts and non-stationary trends are already known to contaminate variance-based statistics of these signals, and a dedicated pre-processing method exists because trend information survives in the variance of Poisson-like photonic signals; so the correction must be applied to detrended series, not raw ones.

Later, in the 1980s, several groups around the world started extensive work to understand the origin and role of this ultraweak emission, now called biophotons, coming from living organisms. Biophotons are an endogenous very small production of photons in the visible energy range in and from cells and organisms, and this emission is characteristic of living organisms. cited_works.abstract: Biophotons are an ultra-weak emission of photons in the visible energy range from living matter. In this work, we study the emission from germinating seeds using an experimental technique designed to detect light of extremely small intensity. The emission from lentil seeds and single bean was analyzed during the whole germination process in terms of the different spectral components through low pass filters and the different count distributions in the various stages of the germination process. Although the shape of the emission spectrum appears to be very similar in the two samples used in our experiment, our analysis can highlight the differences present in the two cases. In this way, it was possible to correlate the various types of emissions to the degree of development of the seed during germination.

cited_works.abstract: Detection and measurement of ultra-weak photon emission (UWPE) from biological samples is a promising tool with potential use in several fields such as agriculture, environmental science, food science and biomedicine. A measurement system especially designed to detect UWPE, and an application in sanitary control of natural water resources is presented here. The system was implemented based on a dark-chamber with a photomultiplier module (PMT) cooled with a microprocessor controlled thermoelectric device coupled. The PMT detects the UWPE from the biological sample under measurement. The performance evaluation of the measuring system in terms of dark-noise and bacteria detection was performed in order to assure that it is able to realize UWPE measurements for the proposed application. cited_works.title: Poisson pre-processing of nonstationary photonic signals: Signals with equality between mean and variance
cited_works.abstract: Photonic signals are broadly exploited in communication and sensing and they typically exhibit Poisson-like statistics. In a common scenario where the intensity of the photonic signals is low and one needs to remove a nonstationary trend of the signals for any further analysis, one faces an obstacle: due to the dependence between the mean and variance typical for a Poisson-like process, information about the trend remains in the variance even after the trend has been subtracted, possibly yielding artifactual results in further analyses. Commonly available detrending or normalizing methods cannot cope with this issue. To alleviate this issue we developed a suitable pre-processing method for the signals that originate from a Poisson-like process. In this paper, a Poisson pre-processing method for nonstationary time series with Poisson distribution is developed and tested on computer-generated model data and experimental data of chemiluminescence from human neutrophils and mung seeds. The presented method transforms a nonstationary Poisson signal into a stationary signal with a Poisson distribution while preserving the type of photocount distribution and phase-space structure of the signal. The importance of the suggested pre-processing method is shown in Fano factor and Hurst exponent analysis of both computer-generated model signals and experimental photonic signals. It is demonstrated that our pre-processing method is superior to standard detrending-based methods whenever further signal analysis is sensitive to variance of the signal.

cited_works.title: Short-time fractal analysis of biological autoluminescence
cited_works.abstract: Biological systems manifest continuous weak autoluminescence, which is present even in the absence of external stimuli. Since this autoluminescence arises from internal metabolic and physiological processes, several works suggested that it could carry information in the time series of the detected photon counts. However, there is little experimental work which would show any difference of this signal from random Poisson noise and some works were prone to artifacts due to lacking or improper reference signals. Here we apply rigorous statistical methods and advanced reference signals to test the hypothesis whether time series of autoluminescence from germinating mung beans display any intrinsic correlations. Utilizing the fractional Brownian bridge that employs short samples of time series in the method kernel, we suggest that the detected autoluminescence signal from mung beans is not totally random, but it seems to involve a process with a negative memory. Our results contribute to the development of the rigorous methodology of signal analysis of photonic biosignals.

statement: A sealed, chemically defined luminescent transfer standard circulated among independent UPE laboratories will be reported in absolute units (photons s-1 into 4 pi, 400-650 nm) with a between-laboratory log10 standard deviation at least three times smaller than the between-laboratory log10 standard deviation obtained by the same laboratories on a common biological sample, demonstrating that the field's non-comparability is dominated by the calibration chain rather than by biological variance.

scope.population: At least five independent laboratories that routinely publish UPE measurements, each using its own detector and its own current calibration practice
scope.condition: Two artefacts circulated in a round-robin: (a) a sealed chemical reference emitter - luminol at defined concentration/pH, and a Fe(II)/H2O2 Fenton cell in defined buffer - in a standardised cuvette and holder; (b) a standardised biological sample - a defined mass of Vigna radiata seeds imbibed under a fixed protocol
scope.comparator: The same laboratories' raw instrument-native reports (counts/s or relative light units) for both artefacts, and a light-tight blank of identical geometry
scope.outcome: Absolute emission rate in photons s-1 (4 pi, 400-650 nm) reported by each laboratory for each artefact, with each laboratory's declared uncertainty budget

null_hypothesis: Between-laboratory agreement on the chemical transfer standard is no better than on the biological sample (log10 SD ratio < 3), meaning radiometric calibration is not the dominant source of the field's disagreement and standardisation of the detection chain alone will not deliver comparability.
estimand: Ratio R = SD_log10(absolute rate, biological sample) / SD_log10(absolute rate, chemical standard), across laboratories; secondary estimand: the fraction of participating laboratories able to report an absolute rate at all.
proposed_experiment: Build two sealed transfer artefacts (a luminol cell and a Fe(II)/H2O2 Fenton cell, both in an identical quartz cuvette and light-tight holder, with a certified stable output over the circulation window) plus a matched dark blank, and ship them sequentially to >=5 UPE laboratories with a fixed measurement protocol but no prescribed calibration method. Each laboratory returns raw counts, its stated conversion to photons s-1 (4 pi, 400-650 nm), and its uncertainty budget. Repeat with a standardised mung-bean germination sample prepared identically at each site. Compute the two between-laboratory log10 SDs and their ratio. Pre-register R >= 3 as support and R < 3 as refutation. Anchor the chain to an SI-traceable absolute detector efficiency at one node using SPDC correlated-pair (Klyshko) calibration.

rationale.step: Given by the seed brief: the field states that luminescence-detection papers rarely report light signals in absolute photon numbers and never report detection limits in units of photon emission rate density, precluding any direct sensitivity comparison; and that UPE remains a technical curiosity rather than a reliable biomarker in the absence of standardization.

Chemical luminescence standards are already the accepted way to calibrate a photon-counting detector in this literature: the luminol standard is described as the easiest way to calibrate the PMT of a light-detection device, and absolute chemiluminescence intensities have been estimated by comparison against the luminol standard.

A precedent exists in this corpus for converting a biological UPE measurement to absolute units via a calibrated light source, and that conversion was decisive: absolute bio-emission intensity from frog and sterlet retinas was found to be at least 100x lower than required to produce discrete rod dark noise, which rejected a standing hypothesis. Absolute units, not counts, carried the inferential weight.

Candidate chemical emitters at the right intensity scale are demonstrated in the corpus: non-catalytic disproportionation of hydrogen peroxide in pure water produces detectable ultraweak luminescence, and Fenton-reagent-initiated oxidation produces a dose-dependent autoluminescence signal in yeast culture, so a chemically defined cell can be tuned to the UPE flux regime rather than the bright-chemiluminescence regime.

The failure mode the round-robin targets is documented in the neighbouring low-light field: a systematic review of 74 photobiomodulation papers found 73% reported no information on how light was measured and relied on manufacturer-stated values, with power missing in 41%, beam area in 40%, irradiance in 43% and radiant energy in 74% - and the authors' remedy is a mandatory ten-parameter reporting list. The same remedy is testable in UPE by round-robin.

That UPE laboratories currently publish in non-convertible instrument-native units is directly observable in the corpus: recent measurement papers report emission solely as relative light units from a commercial luminometer, with the RLU asserted to indicate photons per second per square centimetre but no conversion factor, QE curve or collection geometry given.

Computation of the expected effect size. The detected rate is C = Phi * A_eff * g * eta_bar * T, where g is the geometric collection factor, eta_bar the band-averaged quantum efficiency, T the optical transmission and A_eff the emitting area. Reported human-surface UPE spans 1-1000 photons s-1 cm-2 in one source and 10-10^3 in another, i.e. three decades. If g, eta_bar and T each carry an unreported factor-of-3 uncertainty, their product spans 27x (1.4 decades) - about half the observed literature spread - so the round-robin has the dynamic range to separate the metrological from the biological component.

cited_works.title: Chemi- and Bioluminescence of Cyclic Peroxides
cited_works.abstract: Bioluminescence is a phenomenon that has fascinated mankind for centuries. Today the phenomenon and its sibling, chemiluminescence, have impacted society with a number of useful applications in fields like analytical chemistry and medicine, just to mention two. In this review, a molecular-orbital perspective is adopted to explain the chemistry behind chemiexcitation in both chemi- and bioluminescence. First, the uncatalyzed thermal dissociation of 1,2-dioxetane is presented and analyzed to explain, for example, the preference for triplet excited product states and increased yield with larger nonreactive substituents. The catalyzed fragmentation reaction and related details are then exemplified with substituted 1,2-dioxetanone species. In particular, the preference for singlet excited product states in that case is explained. The review also examines the diversity of specific solutions both in Nature and in artificial systems and the difficulties in identifying the emitting species and unraveling the color modulation process. The related subject of excited-state chemistry without light absorption is finally discussed. The content of this review should be an inspiration to human design of new molecular systems expressing unique light-emitting properties. An appendix describing the state-of-the-art experimental and theoretical methods used to study the phenomena serves as a complement.

cited_works.abstract: Abstract— Photo‐irradiation of aqueous basic solutions of soil humic acids and synthetic melanins with UV and visible light (Λ > 320 nm) under oxygen or nitrogen atmospheres generates electronic exicted states and radicals. These processes give rise to a long‐lived chemiluminescence with emission maxima at 480–500, 570 and 615–650 nm, as well as a paramagnetic resonance (EPR) signal with g‐value at 2.006 and Δ H ∼ 3Gs. Chemiluminescence intensity and EPR signals follow multistep kinetics. An increase of the ratio of OD at 260/400 nm and 400/600 nm and a decrease of amplitude of an EPR signal after prolonged photo‐irradiation were observed. Long irradiation also causes a decrease of fluorescence intensity bands with maxima at 535 nm and 495 nm (Λ ex 480 and 400 nm, respectively), and an increase of the short wavelength band with a maximum at 450 nm (Λ ex 260 nm). The data indicate that a complex chain of reactions initiated by reactive species leads to the degradation of the aromatic core of the polymers. Oxygen efficiently enhances the chemiluminescence intensity and the rate of photodegradation. The mechanism of photodegradative oxidation and chemiluminescence probably involves an energy transfer process and singlet oxygen formation. The possibility of its occurrence in nature and its significance are discussed.

The absolute intensity of bio-emission was estimated by the response of the measuring system to a calibrated light source. The intensity of the source, in turn, was quantified by measuring rhodopsin bleaching with single-rod microspectrophotometry. We also measured the frequency of discrete dark waves in rods of the two species with suction pipette recordings. cited_works.title: Stochastic light concentration from 3D to 2D reveals ultraweak chemi- and bioluminescence
cited_works.abstract: For countless applications in science and technology, light must be concentrated, and concentration is classically achieved with reflective and refractive elements. However, there is so far no efficient way, with a 2D detector, to detect photons produced inside an extended volume with a broad or isotropic angular distribution. Here, with theory and experiment, we propose to stochastically transform and concentrate a volume into a smaller surface, using a high-albedo Ulbricht cavity and a small exit orifice through cavity walls. A 3D gas of photons produced inside the cavity is transformed with a 50% number efficiency into a 2D Lambertian emitting orifice with maximal radiance and a much smaller size. cited_works.title: Biological autoluminescence as a noninvasive monitoring tool for chemical and physical modulation of oxidation in yeast cell culture
cited_works.abstract: Normal or excessive oxidative metabolism in organisms is essential in physiological and pathophysiological processes, respectively. Therefore, monitoring of biological oxidative processes induced by the chemical or physical stimuli is nowadays of extreme importance due to the environment overloaded with various physicochemical factors. Current techniques typically require the addition of chemical labels or light illumination, which perturb the samples to be analyzed. Moreover, the current techniques are very demanding in terms of sample preparation and equipment. To alleviate these limitations, we propose a label-free monitoring tool of oxidation based on biological autoluminescence (BAL). We demonstrate this tool on Saccharomyces cerevisiae cell culture. We showed that BAL can be used to monitor chemical perturbation of yeast due to Fenton reagents initiated oxidation-the BAL intensity changes with hydrogen peroxide concentration in a dose-dependent manner. Furthermore, we also showed that BAL reflects the effects of low-frequency magnetic field on the yeast cell culture, where we observed a disturbance of the BAL kinetics in the exposed vs. control case. Our results contribute to the development of novel techniques for label-free, real-time, noninvasive monitoring of oxidative processes and approaches for their modulation.

cited_works.abstract: Lasers and light-emitting diodes are used for a range of biomedical applications with many studies reporting their beneficial effects. cited_works.title: Comparative analysis of ultra-weak photon emission in the 380–630 nm band in germinated seeds watered with different waters
cited_works.abstract: This study evaluates the influence of the physico-energetic quality of water on germination processes and ultra-low biophotonic emission (UPE) of Alfalfa seeds (Medicago sativa L.). The water samples tested included:(1) mains water, (2) reverse osmosis water, (3) commercial mineral water, and (4) water filtered and revitalized by the OJADE Biophotons 369 system, designed to restructure water via a process combining filtration, vortexing and exposure to coherent photonic fields. The seeds were grown in standard germinators and watered daily with different waters throughout the germination phase. Ultra-weak photon emissions were measured using a Berthold LUMAT LB 9508 luminometer, in the spectral range 380–630 nm. The results show that seeds watered with water from the OJADE Biophotons 369 system exhibit significantly higher biophotonic emission than those watered with other types of water. This increase is correlated with enhanced metabolic and bioenergetic activity, suggesting improved efficiency of oxidative phosphorylation and redox signaling processes. Vitalized water thus appears to act as a coherent carrier of photonic energy, promoting intracellular and intercellular light communication in plant tissues. These observations support the hypothesis that the photodynamic structuring of water can influence biological processes through coherent interactions between the electromagnetic fields of water and those of living systems. Further research is needed to determine the underlying mechanisms and the reproducibility of these effects in other plant models.

cited_works.title: Measuring the Human Ultra-Weak Photon Emission Distribution Using an Electron-Multiplying, Charge-Coupled Device as a Sensor

cited_works.title: Imaging Ultraweak Photon Emission from Living and Dead Mice and from Plants under Stress
cited_works.abstract: The phenomenon of biological ultraweak photon emission (UPE), that is, extremely low-intensity emission (10 − 10 3 photons/cm 2 /sec) in the spectral range of 200 − 1000 nm, has been observed in all living systems that have been examined. Here we report experiments that exemplify the ability of novel imaging systems to detect variations in UPE for a set of physiologically important scenarios. We use EMCCD and CCD cameras to capture single visible-wavelength photons with low noise and quantum efficiencies higher than 90%. Our investigation reveals significant contrast between the UPE from live vs. dead mice. In plants we observed that an increase in temperature and injuries both caused an increase in UPE intensity. Moreover, chemical treatments modified the UPE emission characteristics of plants, particularly the application of an anesthetic (benzocaine) to injury, which showed the highest emission among the compounds tested. As a result, UPE imaging provides the possibility of non-invasive label-free imaging of vitality in animals and the responses of plants to stress.

statement: The wavelength-band ratios that the human-UPE literature uses to discriminate clinical groups are artefacts of the detector's spectral response: recomputing the published 495 nm / 550 nm cut-off-filter ratio after correcting for the measured (not nominal) filter transmission and the detector's per-band quantum efficiency changes the ratio by more than the reported between-group difference, and the healthy-versus-patient discrimination does not survive the correction.

scope.population: Adult humans, fingertip and dorsal-hand surface UPE, healthy controls versus a defined clinical group (common cold, or type-2 diabetes)
scope.condition: Cut-off-filter or bandpass photon counting over 400-700 nm with per-band QE and per-filter transmission measured on the actual instrument
scope.comparator: The same raw photocount data analysed without spectral-response correction, i.e. the published analysis
scope.outcome: Corrected band ratio and its between-group difference with 95% CI, versus the uncorrected band ratio and its between-group difference

null_hypothesis: The spectral-response correction shifts the band ratios by less than the between-group difference and the group discrimination survives with its effect size substantially intact, in which case the spectral-information claim is robust to the metrology gap and H11 is strengthened rather than undermined.
estimand: Delta_corrected - Delta_uncorrected, where Delta is the standardised between-group difference in the band ratio; and the correction factor C = eta_bar(band A)/eta_bar(band B) applied to each ratio.
proposed_experiment: Re-run the two-hand cut-off-filter protocol on matched healthy and clinical cohorts (n >= 20 per group), but measure on the actual instrument: (i) eta(lambda) at 10 nm resolution against an SPDC- or calibrated-source-referenced standard, (ii) each filter's transmission spectrum on the same optical path, (iii) the dark spectrum. Compute band ratios twice from identical raw counts - once as published, once fully corrected - and compare the two between-group effect sizes with a paired bootstrap on the same subjects. Independently repeat the spectral measurement with an EMCCD behind a liquid-crystal tunable filter to obtain a correction-independent spectrum on the same hands in the same session.

rationale.step: The discriminating study itself publishes its instrument's per-band quantum efficiencies: 27% (290-395 nm), 23% (395-455 nm), 15% (455-495 nm), 6% (495-550 nm), 3% (550 nm and above), and reports its discrimination as a photon-emission ratio between the 550 nm and 495 nm filters.

Computation. An uncorrected count ratio between two bands is the true photon-number ratio multiplied by eta_bar(A)/eta_bar(B). For the 455-495 nm versus 495-550 nm pair that factor is 15/6 = 2.5; for the 395-455 nm versus >550 nm pair it is 23/3 = 7.7. The published between-group differences in such ratios are far smaller than 2.5x, so any inter-instrument difference in QE roll-off - or any error in the assumed effective band edges - is large enough to create or destroy the reported discrimination.

Correcting only with manufacturer-stated transmission values is current practice and is insufficient: a plant-UPE study explicitly normalised measured photon counts by each filter's manufacturer-provided average transmission, and the same study reports that PMT photocathode radiant-sensitivity limits prevented accurate analysis over 700-720 nm.

Independent confirmation that instrument spectral response, not source spectrum, dominates the reported band content: a 2026 re-analysis of head UPE shows photons below 600 nm are strongly attenuated by scalp and skull while longer wavelengths fall largely outside the effective spectral sensitivity of the PMTs used, so the recovered 'spectrum' is a product of two steep and opposite roll-offs.

The measurement is buildable now with better spectral control than cut-off filters: an EMCCD behind a liquid-crystal tunable filter has already been used to record human-hand UPE at 400, 450, 500, 550, 600, 650 and 700 nm, and the authors themselves note that non-uniform spectral transmittance of the spectrograph is the limiting factor to be fixed.
The clinical stakes are concrete because band-ratio and spectral features feed published diagnostic claims for type-2 diabetes and for traditional-medicine subtyping.

cited_works.title: Spectral discrimination between healthy people and cold patients using spontaneous photon emission
cited_works.abstract: In this paper, ultra-weak photon emission (UPE) was used to distinguish cold patients from healthy subjects. The UPE intensity of fingertips of two hands from healthy subjects and cold patients was measured using a two-hand UPE detecting system and a group of cut-off filters. We found a significant difference in the maximum spectral peak and photon emission ratio between the filter of 550nm and 495nm, which can be used in distinguish cold patients from healthy people. Methods and results in this work could be useful for developing a new optical diagnostic tool for early disease diagnosis in the future.

Two typical photochemical signaling responses involve the emission of volatile organic compounds and light. The emission of certain leaf wound volatiles and light are mutually dependent upon oxygen which is subsequently required for the wound-induced lipoxygenase reactions that trigger the formation of fatty acids and hydroperoxides; ultimately leading to photon emission by chlorophyll molecules. Leaves were mechanically wounded after two hours of dark adaptation in aerobic and anaerobic conditions. cited_works.title: Revisiting Claims of Extracranial Biophoton Detection from the Human Brain
cited_works.abstract: Ultraweak photon emission, also referred to as biological autoluminescence or biophoton emission, is the spontaneous emission of extremely low levels of light from a broad range of biological systems. Recent studies have reported that UPE measured extracranially can serve as a potential noninvasive biomarker of brain activity. Here, we show that this interpretation suffers from serious problems. We show that, when observed under properly dark conditions, the UPE from the head is much weaker than what is reported in certain papers on "brain UPE" from human heads. We also show that the large signals reported in these studies can be explained by background light contamination. Furthermore, photons with wavelengths <600 nm are strongly attenuated by scalp and skull tissues, and longer wavelengths fall largely outside the effective spectral sensitivity of the photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) used. As a consequence, even if UPE from the head is detected under properly background-free conditions, it is likely to be dominated by emission from the scalp rather than from the brain, certainly as long as PMTs are used. Our results emphasize the importance of careful experimental design to make genuine progress on this important question.

Our results emphasize the importance of careful experimental design to make genuine progress on this important question.

statement: A UPE-based diagnostic classifier trained at one site loses more than half its AUC when applied to a second site using a different detector class, and re-expressing the same features in absolute, spectrally-corrected units (photons s-1 cm-2 per band) recovers at least half of the lost AUC - showing that the field's diagnostic non-transfer is dominated by the missing calibration chain rather than by the biology.

scope.population: Adults with early-stage type-2 diabetes and matched healthy controls (n >= 60 per site), fingertip and dorsal-hand surface UPE
scope.condition: Two independent sites, deliberately different detector classes (cooled PMT photon counter at site A, EMCCD at site B), identical sampling protocol, dark adaptation and anatomical landmarks
scope.comparator: Same classifier evaluated (i) within-site out-of-sample, (ii) cross-site on raw instrument-native counts, (iii) cross-site on absolute spectrally-corrected features
scope.outcome: Out-of-sample AUC in each of the three settings, with 95% CI by site-level bootstrap

null_hypothesis: Absolute-unit re-expression recovers less than half the lost cross-site AUC (recovery fraction < 0.5), meaning the non-transfer is driven by biological, protocol or population differences and calibration is not the binding constraint - which would remove the metrology explanation for the field's diagnostic irreproducibility.
estimand: Recovery fraction R = (AUC_cross_absolute - AUC_cross_raw) / (AUC_within - AUC_cross_raw), with 95% CI.
proposed_experiment: Prospective two-site study with deliberately mismatched detector classes. Site A (cooled PMT, 300-650 nm) and Site B (EMCCD, 400-900 nm) each recruit >=60 early-stage T2D and >=60 matched controls under one shared clinical and dark-adaptation protocol. Both sites measure eta(lambda), dark rate, dead time, filter transmission and collection geometry in-house against a common transfer standard, and archive raw counts. Train a locked classifier at Site A; evaluate within-site out-of-sample, then cross-site twice - once on raw counts, once after converting both sites' archived raw counts to photons s-1 cm-2 per band. rationale.step: Given by the seed brief: the field lists the absence of standardized protocols for clinical measurement among its key experimental constraints, and states that UPE remains a technical curiosity rather than a reliable biomarker without standardization.

Single-site UPE diagnostic claims for type-2 diabetes exist and are the natural training set: UPE has been reported to distinguish healthy subjects from type-2 diabetes patients, proposed as a non-invasive tool for detecting early-stage type-2 diabetes, and combined with plasma metabolomics for subtyping pre-diabetes.

The field has never had an evaluation instrument for this kind of claim: a systematic review of 56 included human-UPE studies (1 RCT, 27 CCT, 28 observational) concluded that a tool for systematically evaluating this bio-evaluation methodology is not currently available and would be worth developing - i.e. no site-transfer criterion exists.

The two detector classes named differ in exactly the parameters that would break raw-count transfer: PMT arms in this literature run at QE ~0.23 with tens of dark counts per second, while EMCCD arms run at QE >0.90 with dark current four orders of magnitude lower, and each has a different spectral weighting.

Computation of the expected AUC damage. A classifier boundary on raw counts is a threshold on C = Phi * A_eff * g * eta_bar * T. Moving to a detector with a different eta_bar rescales C multiplicatively and, because eta_bar is wavelength-dependent, differentially across features - so a linear boundary in raw-count feature space is both translated and sheared. A 2-4x multiplicative shift with a differential band weighting of up to 2.5x (from published per-band QE of 15% versus 6%) is more than enough to push a boundary tuned to a within-site separation of well under one decade to chance. Absolute-unit re-expression removes the multiplicative term exactly and the shear to the accuracy of the measured eta(lambda), which is why R is the informative quantity.

Absolute-unit reporting is achievable at both sites with existing hardware and existing precedent: absolute bio-emission intensity has been obtained by referencing a photon-counting system to a calibrated light source, and national metrology institutes provide traceable or absolute calibration of single-photon detectors and sources.

cited_works.abstract: In this review we present the potentialities and the achievements of the use of non-classical photon-number correlations in twin-beam states for many applications, ranging from imaging to metrology. Photon-number correlations in the quantum regime are easily produced and are rather robust against unavoidable experimental losses, and noise in some cases, if compared to the entanglement, where losing one photon can completely compromise the state and its exploitable advantages. Here, we will focus on quantum enhanced protocols in which only phase-insensitive intensity measurements (photon-number counting) are performed, which allow probing the transmission/absorption properties of a system, leading, for example, to innovative target detection schemes in a strong background. In this framework, one of the advantages is that the sources experimentally available emit a wide number of pair-wise correlated modes, which can be intercepted and exploited separately, for example by many pixels of a camera, providing a parallelism, essential in several applications, such as wide-field sub-shot-noise imaging and quantum enhanced ghost imaging. Finally, non-classical correlation enables new possibilities in quantum radiometry, e.g. the possibility of absolute calibration of a spatial resolving detector from the on-off single-photon regime to the linear regime in the same setup.
